summary:
The DPRK Criminal Code of 1950, revised in 2009, appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts. Two provisions nonetheless leave enforcement to official discretion: Article 193 bans the import, keeping and distribution of "decadent culture", including sexual recordings, and Article 262 bans collective "obscene activities". Neither is defined in terms that constrain how it is applied.

The US State Department's 2022 human rights report reaches the same conclusion, that no specific law criminalises same-sex conduct, and adds that the regime's total control leaves no space for LGBT life. The same department's 2020 report states that no reliable information on LGBT persons exists and that the repression of all civil society is the dominant human-rights reality.

Changing the sex marker on a birth certificate or citizen card is technically possible under "unavoidable circumstances": an application to the People's Security Agency together with a state forensic medical evaluation, with surgical intervention required in practice. No law explicitly bans gender-affirming care, but the under-resourced health system makes hormones and surgery effectively inaccessible.

Article 8 of the Family Law states that marriage may be done only between one man and one woman; as of 2026 no North Korean law recognises same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. Same-sex couples could not legally adopt children as of the 2020 State Department report. The Constitution, last revised 2024, does not address discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no provisions exist in North Korean law prohibiting such discrimination.

Official hostility is documented. A 2014 KCNA commentary rejected the UN Commission of Inquiry's report as a political fabrication and attacked commissioner Michael Kirby with a homophobic slur, evidence of hostility toward homosexuality even while the state denies its existence. A 2014 KCNA statement denied homosexuality's existence outright.

Violence records are sparse and dated. A 2023 South Korean Ministry of Unification report cites defector testimony that at least one male detainee in a detention camp was secretly executed for homosexuality in 2014. A 2011 Korea Times report, sourced to Free North Korea Radio, claimed the execution of a lesbian couple, a North Korean woman and a Japanese woman, for capitalist influence and corruption of public morals. No documented state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people is recorded by Outright International beyond these accounts; the most recent documented case in this record is from 2014, with no later instance documented.

Defector accounts indicate a climate of forced concealment. Jang Young-jin, a novelist who defected in the late 1990s, was forcibly outed and is the first publicly known gay defector; an openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017. The BBC's 2024 feature documents how a collective-over-individual regime forces DPRK sexual minorities into silent self-suppression. New laws, including the Pyongyang Cultural Protection Act, tighten control as of that reporting.

No registration route for LGBTI organisations exists.
tangentialFactors:
The legal picture is defined less by statute than by the absence of information. The US State Department's 2020 report states there is no reliable information on LGBT persons in the DPRK, and the regime's repression of all civil society is the dominant human-rights reality. Outright International records no registration route for LGBTI organisations.

State messaging on homosexuality is contradictory: the regime denies its existence while deploying homophobic insult against international critics, as in the 2014 KCNA attack on Michael Kirby. This suggests exposure as LGBT would be treated as a political or moral matter at official discretion rather than under a defined offence.

Violence figures in this record rest on defector testimony and secondary reporting rather than direct documentation, and the most recent dated execution account is from 2014. No per-capita or population context is available for these raw counts, and they should not be read as a prevalence measure.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Articles 193 and 262 have been applied against same-sex conduct or gender-nonconforming presentation is not sourced here; the inventory records the provisions' text and their undefined scope, not their use.

The execution accounts from 2011 and 2014 rest on defector testimony and secondary reporting; independent corroboration is unresolved in this record.

Entry, visa and border-screening treatment of trans travellers into the DPRK is not covered by any source in this inventory and remains unsourced.
